broccoli-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-mar.title: Broccoli, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is an edible flower head from the Brassicaceae family, originally native to the Mediterranean region. Fresh florets are commonly sautéed in butter or margarine, which preserves their vivid green color and enhances flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
It is believed that broccoli was first cultivated in ancient Rome.
Edible parts include not only the florets but also stems, leaves, and even the roots.
Cooking broccoli in butter retains more vitamin C than boiling in water.
In Japan, broccoli is often served as tempura, a light batter made from rice flour.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: One cup of cooked broccoli provides over 100 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked broccoli with a modest amount of butter contains about 55 kcal per 100 g, making it a weight‑friendly choice.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to broccoli, ranging from itching to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can be fermented by gut bacteria and cause flatulence.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Large amounts of raw broccoli may interfere with iodine absorption, which is relevant for individuals on thyroid medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté broccoli in butter or margarine over medium heat for 5‑7 minutes until tender yet crisp. Add garlic, lemon juice, or your favorite herbs. Serve as a side dish, in salads, pasta, or baked casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh broccoli in a perforated bag in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C, where it stays fresh for up to 5 days. Cooked broccoli should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3 days. Discard any heads with yellow or slimy spots.

cereal-or-granola-bar-kashi-crunchy.title: Kashi Crunchy Cereal or Granola Bar

content.title: About
content.content: Kashi Crunchy is a whole‑grain cereal/granola bar that combines whole oats, wheat, barley, sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds and a modest amount of sweetener. It is marketed as a nutritious on‑the‑go snack with high fiber and protein, free from artificial flavors and colors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar is produced by Kashi, a brand known for whole‑grain products.
It contains whole oat flakes, whole wheat and barley, plus sunflower and pumpkin seeds.
The standard version contains gluten, but a gluten‑free variant is also offered.
Kashi Crunchy is Non‑GMO Project Verified, meaning no genetically modified ingredients are used.
Each bar is individually wrapped for convenient portable snacking.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal digestive function and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Nuts and seeds provide about 5 g of protein per serving, useful for muscle repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Sunflower and pumpkin seeds are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains supply B1, B2 and niacin, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Compared with many sweet bars, the amount of added sugar is limited, making it a better option for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Nut and seed allergy
items.content: Sunflower and pumpkin seeds may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The regular version contains wheat; people with celiac disease should choose the gluten‑free version.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One bar provides roughly 200 kcal, so portion size should be considered within daily energy needs.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: A small amount of salt is present; those limiting sodium intake should be aware.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kashi Crunchy can be eaten straight from the wrapper, crumbled over yogurt or kefir, mixed into oatmeal, or used as an energy boost before workouts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Anchovies are small marine fish of the Engraulidae family, found in the warm waters of the Atlantic, Mediterranean and Black Seas. They are commonly sold salted, marinated or canned and add a strong, savory flavor to many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Anchovies are often called “sea salt” because their intense taste enhances the flavor of other ingredients.
They are a staple in Italian cuisine (pizza, puttanesca sauce) and Spanish tapas (anchovy sauce, escarola).
Two main species are used: European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) and California anchovy (Engraulis mordax).
Canned anchovies are usually packed in oil or brine, preserving their softness and aroma.
Anchovies are rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help maintain healthy cholesterol levels and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: About 20 g of complete protein per 100 g, supporting muscle and tissue maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, niacin and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Provides calcium, iron, magnesium and selenium, essential for bones, blood and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Despite their strong flavor, anchovies are relatively low‑calorie when eaten without excess oil.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to seafood may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylactic.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salted and canned anchovies contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension or kidney issues.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination risk
items.content: Like other marine fish, anchovies can accumulate mercury and other toxins; choose reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Anchovies are commonly added to sauces, salads, pastas and pizza. Use them as a flavor enhancer, mash into a paste, or serve whole as a snack. Pairing with oil or lemon brightens their taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened canned anchovies in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3–5 days. Dried salted anchovies should be kept in the fridge to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are dried beans to which a small amount of vegetable fat has been added to improve flavor and texture. They are rich in protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, and provide iron, folate, and magnesium. Kidney beans are commonly used in soups, stews, salads, and vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "kidney" comes from the bean’s characteristic red‑brown spot that resembles a kidney.
Dried beans should be soaked for 6–12 hours before cooking.
Adding fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and gives the beans a richer taste.
Kidney beans are a staple in South American and Caribbean cuisines.
One serving (about 100 g dry beans) provides more than 20 g of protein.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: Kidney beans contain roughly 20 g of protein per 100 g of dry product, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, blood‑sugar regulation, and weight management.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for blood formation, while folate is important for DNA synthesis and anemia prevention.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help maintain heart, muscle, and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic impact after cooking
items.content: When properly prepared, kidney beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Dry beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking lower its level.

items.title: Toxic lectins
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can cause food poisoning; they must be fully cooked.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Higher calorie content due to added fat
items.content: The added vegetable fat increases the energy density, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak the beans for at least 6 hours, rinse well, then boil for 60–90 minutes until tender. Add them to soups, chili, salads, vegetarian patties, or serve as a side dish. The added fat makes the beans richer, so they can also be sautéed briefly after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep for 1–2 years. Cooked beans should be refrigerated and used within 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-not-eaten.title: Potato, roasted, fresh, peel not eaten, with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potato is made from fresh tubers that are peeled and fried in butter. It features a golden crust, tender interior, and the rich aroma of butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is one of the most widely consumed vegetables worldwide.
Frying in butter gives a richer flavor compared with most vegetable oils.
There are many cutting styles—wedges, cubes, rounds—each providing a different texture.
Roasted potatoes are often served as a side dish with meat or fish.
Proper frying creates a crisp crust that locks moisture inside.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Vitamin C contributes to immune support and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs give sustained energy and help keep you feeling full.

items.title: Beta‑carotene
items.content: Yellow and orange varieties contain provitamin A, beneficial for vision.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: A modest amount of fiber aids digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Butter frying increases the dish’s calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Butter contains saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Very high frying temperatures may produce acrylamide, a potential harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone dish, a side to meat or fish, or as a snack. Sprinkle with fresh herbs, spices, or a pinch of salt for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked roasted potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness.

tofu-and-vegetables-excluding-carrots-br.title: Tofu with vegetables without carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, no potatoes, with soy sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Tofu is a soy‑based product made by coagulating soy milk. In this dish tofu is combined with a mix of vegetables, deliberately excluding carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens and potatoes, and is finished with a soy‑based sauce (ID 2243). The meal is rich in plant protein, vitamins and minerals, and is suitable for vegetarians and vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tofu is often called “plant meat” because of its texture and ability to absorb flavors.
The soy sauce used is traditionally fermented for several months, giving it a deep umami taste.
Excluding carrots, broccoli and leafy greens makes the dish easier on people sensitive to certain fibers.
Tofu contains all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
The dish can be quickly prepared in a skillet or steamer, preserving most nutrients.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu provides about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Tofu is mainly composed of poly‑ and monounsaturated fats, which are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of calcium and iron
items.content: Coagulated tofu is often calcium‑enriched, and soy naturally supplies iron important for blood health.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Fermented soy sauce contains probiotic cultures that can benefit intestinal health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The absence of starchy potatoes makes the dish suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products, including tofu and soy sauce.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Soy contains phytates, which in large amounts may reduce mineral absorption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stir‑fry the tofu and vegetables briefly in a little oil, add the soy sauce at the end of cooking. Serve hot as a main dish, in Buddha bowls, or over rice or quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tofu in an airtight container covered with fresh water in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, changing the water daily. Store vegetables separately in a dry place. Unopened soy sauce can be kept in a cool, dark pantry; once opened, refrigerate.
